that LCS had no effect (Maersk et al., 2012), or reduced clinical indicators of NAFLD (Campos et al., 2015) when SSB was replaced
with LCS-containing beverages.
Type 2 diabetes
Observational studies suggest elevated risk of type 2 diabetes with higher LCS intake when reported as servings per day (RR ¼ 1.03,
95%CI 1.01–1.05, n ¼ 4 studies) or for comparisons of lowest vs. highest quartile’s of intake (RR ¼ 1.14, 95%CI 1.05–1.25, n ¼ 9
studies) (Azad et al., 2017). In a scoping review, positive associations were also reported between LCS consumed in beverages and
the risk of T2DM, but ﬁndings were mixed when overall LCS intake was considered (Lohner et al., 2017). This highlights the impor-
tance of assessing the form of LCS being consumed. Nonetheless, this is an area of particular risk for reverse causation, where people
with diabetes are more likely to use LCS to improve glycemic control. Findings are also subject to publication bias, inconsistency,
and imprecision in pooled estimates (Sievenpiper et al., 2017).
